source.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
source.authors: Qi Zhang; Yi-Fei Wang; Jing-Yi Cui; Xiang Pan; Qi Lei; S. Jegelka; Yi-Sen Wang

page_placements.theme: Consequences of superposition: adversarial vulnerability, noise sensitivity, interference errors

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemantic and monosemantic features, but its experiments measure downstream classification robustness, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, why they do so, or how often they do.
record.gate_note: The paper compares polysemantic and monosemantic feature methods on noisy and shifted-data tasks. Those results concern a related robustness question, not the neuron-level claims in V1–V7. Rows below record the separately reported Table 1 linear-probing accuracies; the paper also reports other robustness results, which do not test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study takes the polysemantic/monosemantic distinction as given and uses methods to make features monosemantic: NCL and a TopK SAE on SimCLR ResNet-18 features, plus NCE finetuning and MonoLoRA. It then reports only downstream robustness (linear-probe and finetuning accuracy, alignment scores). It never measures how many units are polysemantic in any model, or how that share changes with method. The monosemanticity of NCL and SAE features is cited from Wang et al. (2024) and Gao et al. (2024), not re-measured. The superposition toy model is built to produce polysemantic features and is used to compare robustness, so it does not test V3's causal claim. Figures 1(a) and 4(a) show single examples of mixed-class top activations in a CL dimension, and Figure 4(c) gives a semantic-consistency score. These are illustrations or robustness diagnostics, not a rate of polysemantic neurons, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that monosemantic features improve robustness to label noise, input noise, distribution shift, few-shot finetuning and LLM finetuning. They argue this challenges the assumed accuracy–interpretability tradeoff.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares contrastive learning, non-negative contrastive learning, and sparse-autoencoder features for robustness; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization or SoLU procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with dataset, label-noise rate, feature method, and robustness setting. For noisy linear probing, gains generally grow at higher noise rates, though not uniformly across methods and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on NCL and SAE features keep clean accuracy close to CL features but gain substantially under heavy label noise, up to +13.7 points (NCL, ImageNet-100, 90% noise). Gains also appear under input noise and on Sketch/Stylized shifts (Fig. 2), in few-shot and noisy finetuning with NCE (Fig. 3), and in alignment retention with MonoLoRA (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features made monosemantic by NCL or SAE are more robust to label noise, input noise and distribution shift than polysemantic contrastive features, at little clean-accuracy cost.

fits_no_version.finding: In the superposition toy model (n=40, m=20, S=0.2), superposed features score higher on clean data (0.58 vs 0.50) but lower under 90% label noise and under input noise (Fig. 5b). The theory shows the separability ordering flips at noise rate 0.25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition trades clean accuracy for lower robustness to noise.

record.problems: Table 1 reports no uncertainty estimates. The recorded results are classification accuracies, not direct measurements of neuron-level semantic coherence or polysemantic-neuron prevalence.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap is filled with every numeric linear-probing result in Table 1. Other separately reported results are omitted: input-noise and real-world shifts (Figure 2), few-shot and noisy finetuning (Figure 3), salient-feature consistency (Figure 4), MonoLoRA results (Table 2), toy-model plots (Figure 5), and the additional robust-loss plot (Figure 6). These results concern robustness rather than the listed neuron-level claim versions.

untested.parts: No measurement of how many image-classifier neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Figures 1(a) and 4(a) show only illustrative top-activated samples for single dimensions of a SimCLR ResNet-18 projector output.
No language-model MLP neuron analysis. The MonoLoRA work reports sparsity of LoRA activations, not polysemanticity.
The Elhage toy model is used with superposition built in to compare robustness. Whether superposition causes polysemanticity is not tested.

Clean-label accuracy of NCL and SAE features is close to CL (-0.1 to -1.7 points). However, the share of polysemantic units under each method is not measured in this paper, so the claim that the share is lowered is untested here.
Uses a single monosemanticity score (semantic consistency, top-activation class purity). It does not compare activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses is close, but the study does use monosemanticity-inducing methods as its tool, so T4/uses_without_test fits better. All Table 1 rows correctly carry versions ['none']; the values match the table. The text says 9.2% gain on 'CIFAR-10', but Table 1 reports it for CIFAR-100. There are no uncertainty estimates. Figure 4(c) semantic consistency is 9.40 vs 14.90 (CIFAR-100) and 16.32 vs 22.48 (ImageNet-100), wrong vs correct samples. It is a robustness diagnostic, not a prevalence measure.

versions.untested_parts: No neuron-level responses in image classifiers or examples such as InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55 are measured.
No language-model MLP neuron responses to tokens or contexts are measured.
The toy model is built using a superposition setup, but the study does not test whether superposition causes polysemanticity in trained networks.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
The study compares methods intended to promote monosemanticity, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or compare activation functions/architectures on that measure.
No investigation of whether canonical mixed-response neurons share a coherent feature or job.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

relation.reason: It takes the poly/mono distinction as given and uses methods that induce monosemanticity as tools for robustness.

tranche.reason: The paper makes features monosemantic (NCL, TopK SAE, NCE finetuning, MonoLoRA) and reports only downstream robustness. It does not measure how common polysemantic neurons are, and it takes NCL/SAE monosemanticity from prior work rather than measuring it here. So it tests no version.

source_check.notes: Rows match Table 1 (ImageNet-100, 90% label noise) and Figure 1(b). In Table 1 the NCL +9.2 at 90% noise is under CIFAR-100; the body text says CIFAR-10, likely a typo. Polysemantic-neuron versions are not tested, so empty verdicts are right. The record's venue 'ICLR 2024' conflicts with the Oct 2024 arXiv date.
